'''Mostafa Chamran Savehi''' ({{langx|fa|مصطفی چمران ساوه‌ای}}; 2 October 1932 &ndash; 21 June 1981) was an Iranian [[scientist]], [[politician]], and [[Guerrilla warfare|guerrilla]], best known for serving as the first [[Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics (Iran)|defense minister]] of [[Iranian Revolution|post-revolutionary]] Iran.

In 1980, Chamran was elected to the [[Islamic Consultative Assembly|Iranian Majles]], representing [[Tehran]]. That same year, he commanded a [[paramilitary]] unit in the [[Iran–Iraq War]], known as the "[[Irregular Warfare Headquarters]]". He was later [[Killed in action|killed]] on the frontlines.

==Early life and education==
Chamran was born into a religious [[Persians|Persian]] family on 2 October 1932 in Tehran.<ref name=vida>{{cite web|author=Vida Moezzinia|title=Dr. Mostafa Chamran|url=http://iichs.org/index_en.asp?id=1609&doc_cat=16|publisher=IICHS|access-date=17 February 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130227045553/http://iichs.org/index_en.asp?id=1609&doc_cat=16|archive-date=27 February 2013|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Dominique Avon|author2=Anaïs-Trissa Khatchadourian|title=Hezbollah. A History of the "Party of God"|date=2012|publisher=Harvard University Press |location=Cambridge, MA|isbn=9780674067523|page=198|url=https://doi.org/10.4159/harvard.9780674067523|doi=10.4159/harvard.9780674067523}}</ref> His younger brother was [[Mehdi Chamran]], who later served as the chairman of the [[Islamic City Council of Tehran|City Council of Tehran]]. 

Chamran studied at [[Alborz High School]], while also receiving religious education from [[Mahmoud Taleghani]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Shahid Mostafa Chamran has been known for his life of sacrifices|url=http://abna.ir/data.asp?lang=3&Id=193400|access-date=17 February 2013|work=ABNA|date=26 June 2010|archive-date=13 April 2013|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130413000942/http://abna.ir/data.asp?lang=3&Id=193400|url-status=dead}}</ref> After graduating from the [[University of Tehran]] with a [[bachelor's degree]] in [[electromechanics]], he moved to the [[United States]] for higher education under an Imperial Iranian government [[scholarship]], obtaining a [[Master of Science|master of science]] in [[Electrical engineering|electricial engineering]] from [[Texas A&M University]].<ref name="vida" /><ref>{{cite book|title=An integrator based on motion and electrostatic charge. (Book, 1959)|publisher=[WorldCat.org]|oclc=5974555}}</ref> In 1963, Chamran obtained his [[Doctor of Philosophy|doctorate]] in electrical engineering and [[Plasma (physics)|plasma physics]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/Pubs/Dissertations/Years/1963.html|title=PhD Dissertations; EECS at UC Berkeley|publisher=CS|date=9 January 2013|access-date=17 February 2013}}</ref> He was subsequently employed as a research staff scientist at [[Bell Labs|Bell Laboratories]] and later at [[NASA]]'s [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]].<ref name="bezahra">{{cite book|author=Scott Peterson|title=Let the Swords Encircle Me: Iran--A Journey Behind the Headlines|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781416597285|url-access=registration|date=21 September 2010|publisher=Simon & Schuster|isbn=978-1-4165-9739-1|pages=[https://archive.org/details/isbn_9781416597285/page/701 701]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.lib.ir/book/80662307/Selfconstruction-and-development/|title=Self-construction and development (author Mostafa Chamran) - کتابخانه تخصصی جهاد و شهادت (موسسه فرهنگی روایت سیره شهدا)|last=دارالحدیث|first=موسسه علمی فرهنگی|website=www.lib.ir|access-date=24 September 2017}}</ref>

==Career==

=== Revolutionary activities ===

==== Guerilla training ====
In the early 1960s, Chamran became a prominent member of the [[Freedom Movement of Iran|Freedom Movement of Iran (FMI)]], a pro-[[Islamic democracy|democratic]], anti-[[Mohammad Reza Pahlavi|Shah]] political organization led by [[Mehdi Bazargan]].<ref name="vida" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Mehdi Bazargan's biography|url=http://www.bazargan.info/la_english/english.htm|work=Bazargan website|access-date=3 August 2013}}</ref> He belonged to the party's [[Islamic socialism|left-wing religious]] revolutionary bloc alongside [[Ebrahim Yazdi]], [[Sadegh Ghotbzadeh]] and [[Ali Shariati]], all of whom had studied at [[Western world|Western]] universities.<ref name="disrel">{{cite book|author1=Houchang Chehabi|author2=Rula Jurdi Abisaab|author3=Centre for Lebanese Studies (Great Britain)|title=Distant Relations: Iran and Lebanon in the Last 500 Years|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=elHww0W0ZO4C&pg=PA182|date=2 April 2006|publisher=I.B.Tauris|isbn=978-1-86064-561-7|pages=182}}</ref>

Chamran went to [[Cuba]] to attend a [[Training camp|military camp]].<ref name="Sepehr Zabih 84–94">{{cite journal|author=Sepehr Zabih|title=Aspects of Terrorism in Iran|journal=Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science|date=September 1982|volume=463|series=International Terrorism|pages=84–94|doi=10.1177/0002716282463001007|jstor=1043613|s2cid=145391253}}</ref> In December 1963, he, Ghotbzadeh, and Yazdi traveled from the [[United States]] to [[United Arab Republic|Egypt]], where they received training in [[Guerrilla warfare|guerilla warfare]].<ref name="yehudit">{{cite web|last=Barsky|first=Yehudit|title=Hizballah|url=http://www.ajc.org/atf/cf/%7B42D75369-D582-4380-8395-D25925B85EAF%7D/Hizballah_052003.pdf|work=The American Jewish Committee|access-date=5 August 2013|format=Terrorism Briefing|date=May 2003|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029184824/http://www.ajc.org/atf/cf/%7B42D75369-D582-4380-8395-D25925B85EAF%7D/Hizballah_052003.pdf|archive-date=29 October 2013}}</ref><ref name="abaw">{{cite journal|author=Abbas William Samii|title=The Shah's Lebanon policy: the role of SAVAK|journal=Middle Eastern Studies|year=1997|volume=33|issue=1|pages=66–91|doi=10.1080/00263209708701142}}</ref> There, they met with Egyptian authorities to propose establishing an anti-Shah organization in the country called the {{ill|Special Organization for Unity and Action|fa|سازمان مخصوص اتحاد و عمل}} or SAMA, with Chamran leading its military branch.<ref name="disrel" />

Upon Chamran's return to the United States in 1965, he founded a group called "Red Shi'ism" in [[San Jose, California|San Jose]], aimed at training [[Far-left politics|far-left]] [[Shia Islamism|Islamist]] [[militant]]s; his brother Mehdi was an early member.<ref name="yehudit" /> In 1968, he helped establish another anti-Shah and Islamist organization, the Muslim Students' Association of America (MSA), which was led by Yazdi.<ref name="yehudit" /> The MSA soon had branches in the [[United Kingdom]] and [[France]].<ref name="yehudit" />

==== Arab world ====
In 1971, Chamran left the United States for [[Lebanon]]<ref name="yehudit" /> to join the [[Palestine Liberation Organization]] and [[Amal Movement]].<ref name="Sepehr Zabih 84–94"/> He became a leading figure of the revolutionary Islamic movement in the Middle East, organizing and training guerrilla forces in [[Algeria]], Egypt, and [[Ba'athist Syria|Syria]]. During [[Lebanese Civil War]], he actively cooperated with [[Musa al-Sadr]] and became known as his "right-hand man".<ref name="ostovar">{{cite thesis|author=Afshon P. Ostovar|title=Guardians of the Islamic Revolution Ideology, Politics, and the Development of Military Power in Iran (1979–2009)|url=http://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/handle/2027.42/64683/afshon_1.pdf;jsessionid=DF7BFA33BF18FF73E9117CB0504F14E1?sequence=1|location=University of Michigan|degree=PhD|year=2009}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Musa al Sadr: The Untold Story|url=http://www.aawsat.net/2008/05/article55258754|access-date=5 August 2013|newspaper=Asharq Alawsat|date=31 May 2008|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131019131923/http://www.aawsat.net/2008/05/article55258754|archive-date=19 October 2013}}</ref><ref name="ata">{{cite journal|author=Mohammad Ataie|title=Revolutionary Iran's 1979 endeavor in Lebanon|journal=Middle East Policy|date=Summer 2013|volume=XX|issue=2|doi=10.1111/mepo.12026|pages=137–157|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Chamran, along with Sadegh Ghotbzadeh, was known as part of a clique called the “Syrian mafia” within the inner circle of [[Ruhollah Khomeini]]. There was a reported feud between this group and a [[History of Libya under Muammar Gaddafi#Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya (1977–2011)|Libya]]-friendly faction led by [[Mohammad Montazeri]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Gayn|first=Mark|author-link=Mark Gayn|title=Into the depths of a boiling caldron|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=DCNlAAAAIBAJ&pg=1340,5195980&dq=mohammad+montazeri&hl=en|access-date=27 July 2013|newspaper=Edmonton Journal|date=20 December 1979}}</ref>

=== Post-revolutionary Iran ===

==== Political appointments ====
Following the [[Iranian Revolution]], Chamran returned to Iran in February 1979 and was appointed Deputy Prime Minister for Revolutionary Affairs in the [[Interim Government of Iran (1979)|cabinet]] of [[Mehdi Bazargan]].<ref name="tpp79">{{cite news|title=Iran Unleashes Might on Kurds|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=iuoeAAAAIBAJ&pg=6542,221594&dq=mostafa+chamran&hl=en|access-date=8 August 2013|newspaper=The Pittsburgh Press|date=2 September 1979|agency=UPI|location=Tehran}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Kurds claim town siege|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=UvgiAAAAIBAJ&pg=805,2321889&dq=mostafa+chamran&hl=en|access-date=8 August 2013|newspaper=The Palm Beach Post|date=17 August 1979}}{{Dead link|date=March 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> He was later appointed [[Ministry of Defence and Armed Forces Logistics (Iran)|Minister of Defense]],<ref>{{cite book|author=Sepehr Zabir|title=The Iranian Military in Revolution and War (RLE Iran D)|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TcjmD51dFFMC&pg=PT277|date=23 April 2012|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-136-81270-5|pages=277}}</ref> becoming the first civilian defense minister of the Islamic Republic.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Gregory F. Rose|title=The Post-Revolutionary Purge of Iran's Armed Forces: A Revisionist Assessment|journal=Iranian Studies|date=Spring–Summer 1984|volume=17|issue=2–3|pages=153–194|doi=10.1080/00210868408701627|jstor=4310440}}</ref> As a result of this position, Chamran led military action against a [[1979 Kurdish rebellion in Iran|rebellion]] in [[Kurdistan province|Kurdistan]].<ref name="tpp79" />

In May 1980, Chamran was elected to the [[Islamic Consultative Assembly|Majles]] (parliament) as a representative of Tehran.<ref name="Bak1996">{{cite book|author=Bahman Baktiari|title=Parliamentary Politics in Revolutionary Iran: The Institutionalization of Factional Politics|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Z_jPuuxfIv4C&pg=PA79|access-date=27 July 2013|year=1996|publisher=University Press of Florida|isbn=978-0-8130-1461-6|pages=79}}</ref> That same month, he was appointed by Khomeini to the [[Supreme National Security Council|Supreme Council of National Defense]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Khomenei's hard-liners triumph|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1314&dat=19800512&id=B1ZOAAAAIBAJ&pg=6991,6282811|access-date=4 August 2013|newspaper=The Spokesman Review|date=May 1980|agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

==== Iran-Iraq War ====
When the [[Iran–Iraq War]] began in September 1980, Chamran led an [[irregular warfare]] infantry unit called the "[[Irregular Warfare Headquarters]]".<ref name="bezahra" /> He was [[Wounded in action|wounded]] in the leg during the [[Liberation of Susangerd]].<ref>{{Cite news |last= |date=June 22, 1981 |title=Iranian Guerrilla Leader Is Killed in the War Zone |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/06/22/world/iranian-guerrilla-leader-is-killed-in-the-war-zone.html |access-date=2026-02-27 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

==Death==
Chamran was killed in [[Dehlaviyeh]] on 21 June 1981 during a clash with [[Iraqi Armed Forces|Iraqi forces]].<ref name="vida" /><ref>Bernard Reich, ''Political Leaders of the Contemporary Middle East and North Africa '' [https://books.google.com/books?id=3D5FulN2WqQC&dq=%22chamran+died%22&pg=PA466 p.466]</ref><ref>Daniel Brumberg, ''Reinventing Khomeini'' [https://books.google.com/books?id=Cdjs7HCjIsYC&pg=PA272 p.272]</ref><ref name="ChehabiAbisaab2006">{{cite book|author1=Houchang Chehabi|author2=Rula Jurdi Abisaab|title=Distant Relations|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=elHww0W0ZO4C&pg=PA208|access-date=19 February 2013|date=2 April 2006|publisher=I.B.Tauris|isbn=978-1-86064-561-7|pages=208}}</ref><ref>Houchang E. Chehabi, ''Iranian Politics and Religious Modernism'' [https://books.google.com/books?id=JJEIQbUnGyYC&pg=PA293 p.293]</ref> The details surrounding his death have remained unclear.<ref name="Lorentz2010">{{cite book|author=John H. Lorentz|title=The A to Z of Iran|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=o-rIhengOn0C&pg=PA69|date=1 April 2010|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-0-8108-7638-5|pages=69}}</ref><ref name="gan2002">{{cite book|author=Manouchehr Ganji|title=Defying the Iranian Revolution: From a Minister to the Shah to a Leader of Resistance|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NboVl-CeYs0C&pg=PA109|access-date=1 August 2013|year=2002|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=978-0-275-97187-8|pages=109}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Augustus R. Norton|title=Hezbollah: A Short History|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=x0MZOnnu8qcC&pg=PA30|date=19 January 2009|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=978-0-691-14107-7|page=30}}</ref> He is buried in the [[Behesht-e Zahra]] cemetery in Tehran.<ref name="bezahra" />

==Personal life==

=== Marriages ===
Chamran married an [[Americans|American]] woman, Tamsen Keyston, in 1961.<ref>{{Cite news |date=27 May 1961 |title=Tamsen Keyston to Wed in Moslem Ceremony |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-san-francisco-examiner/33633194/ |access-date= |work=[[The San Francisco Examiner]] |pages=9}}</ref> They had four children together before divorcing in the early 1970s; one of them, a son named Jamal, died at the age of three in a pool drowning accident in 1973.<ref>{{Cite news |date=9 September 1973 |title=Family Pool Claims Life of Young Boy |url=https://cdnc.ucr.edu/?a=d&d=CCT19730909.1.8&srpos=20&e=-------en--20--1--txt-txIN-Chamran------- |work=[[East Bay Times|Contra Costa Times]] |page=8 |volume=58 |issue=158}}</ref>

During his time in Lebanon, Chamran remarried a [[Lebanese people|Lebanese]] woman, Ghada Jaber, who was also a member of the Amal Movement.<ref>{{cite news|title=Mostafa Chamran's Lebanon converted into Arabic|url=http://www.ibna.ir/vdcds90fsyt0k96.em2y.html|access-date=4 August 2013|work=Iran Book News Agency|date=12 December 2012}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Shaery-Eisenlohr |first=Roschanack |year=2008 |title=Shi'ite Lebanon: Transnational Religion and the Making of National Identities |url=https://ciaotest.cc.columbia.edu/book/cup/0001320/0001320.pdf |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |page=102}}</ref>

==Legacy==
Ayatollah Khomeini publicly proclaimed Chamran as a "proud commander of Islam".<ref name=bezahra/> Chamran was posthumously honoured by having buildings and streets in Iran and Lebanon named after him, including a [[Chamran Expressway|major expressway]].<ref name=bezahra/> A [[Anagnorisma chamrani|species of moth]] was named after him in 2013.<ref>{{Cite journal| author1=M. Esfandiari|author2=P. Gyulai|author3=M. Rabieh|author4=A. Seraj|author5=L. Ronkay|title=''Anagnorisma chamrani'' sp. n. (Lepidoptera, Noctuidae) from Iran|doi=10.3897/zookeys.317.5515|journal=ZooKeys|issue=317| pages=17–25|year=2013|pmid=23950668|pmc=3744136|doi-access=free|bibcode=2013ZooK..317...17G }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=New Anagnorisma Moth Species from Beautiful Binaloud Mountain Iran|url=https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2013/07/130717114500.htm|access-date=8 August 2013|newspaper=Science Daily|date=17 July 2013}}</ref>

=== Media ===
In 2012, Mohsen Alavipour published a Persian-language biography of Chamran.<ref>{{cite news|title=Martyr Chamran's biography book unveiled|url=http://www.taghribnews.com/vdcevo8o.jh8voik1bj.html|access-date=4 August 2013|work=Taqrib News|date=20 June 2012}}</ref> The next year, an English-language biography of Chamran titled ''22: Not a new lifestyle for those who thirst for humanity!'' was published in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{cite news|title=Book on lifestyle of Iranian veteran Chamran published in UK|url=http://www.tehrantimes.com/arts-and-culture/109182-book-on-lifestyle-of-iranian-veteran-chamran-published-in-uk|access-date=8 August 2013|newspaper=Tehran Times|date=10 July 2013|location=Tehran|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131206164414/http://www.tehrantimes.com/arts-and-culture/109182-book-on-lifestyle-of-iranian-veteran-chamran-published-in-uk|archive-date=6 December 2013}}</ref>

In 2014, a film titled ''[[Che (2014 film)|Che]]'' ([[Persian language|Persian]]: چ), directed by [[Ebrahim Hatamikia]], was released to honour Chamran. The film portrays two days in Chamran's life following the Iranian Revolution. In 2017, [[Reza Mirkarimi]] produced an [[Animation|animated film]] about Chamran.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Story Of The Life Of Mostafa Chamran With English Subtitles |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9LaHhynI40E |website=Youtube | date=6 January 2023 |access-date=25 October 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | title=Director Mirkarimi animations to be screened |website=IRNA English | url=https://en.irna.ir/amp/2733581/ |date=9 August 2014 | access-date=25 October 2023}}</ref>
